evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This peer-reviewed study analyzes self-reported survey data from 2,170 U.S. patients (1,839 women, 331 men) in the MyLymeData patient registry who were clinically diagnosed with Lyme disease and remained ill six or more months after antibiotic treatment (persistent/chronic Lyme disease, PLD/CLD). spec.title: Sex Differences in Persistent/Chronic Lyme Disease: Diagnostic Delay, Misdiagnosis, and Functional Impairment
spec.boundary: This simulator models only the sex-disaggregated percentages this peer-reviewed study reports from its own MyLymeData patient registry sample (N=2170; 1839 women, 331 men; dataset dated April 27, 2017), all self-reported by patients already clinically diagnosed with persistent/chronic Lyme disease (illness continuing six or more months after antibiotic treatment). It also includes the study's separate review of what share of women were enrolled across different Lyme disease study designs. It does not and cannot model any dollar cost, lost income, or caregiving-hour figure, because this document reports none. All percentages describe this specific self-selected registry sample, not a general population estimate.

takeaway.patient: This study reported that among 2,170 people in a self-selected patient registry who were clinically diagnosed with persistent/chronic Lyme disease, women were reported to have higher rates than men of being diagnosed at a late stage, being misdiagnosed beforehand with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or a psychiatric condition, and reporting many bed days. The study also found no significant sex difference in rash recollection, lab test positivity, or how well antibiotic treatment worked. These are patterns the study observed in this registry, not a prediction about any individual's own experience.
takeaway.care: In this registry-based study, women with persistent/chronic Lyme disease were reported at significantly higher rates than men for late-stage diagnosis, prior misdiagnosis (especially with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or a psychiatric condition), and high bed-day burden, while rash recollection, lab-test positivity, and antibiotic response/side effects showed no significant sex difference. The misdiagnosis pattern, alongside unchanged lab-positivity rates, suggests the gap traces to clinical interpretation or workup pathway rather than to test results themselves, as the study's own data show.
takeaway.policy: The study found that the female share of patients enrolled in Lyme disease research varied sharply by study design in the sources it reviewed - lower in acute Lyme disease study samples, higher in less-restrictive persistent-illness cohort samples like its own - and that none of the NIH-funded trials it reviewed were designed to analyze sex differences. It also documents statistically significant sex gaps in diagnostic delay, misdiagnosis, and functional impairment within its own persistent-illness cohort. No dollar-denominated burden estimate is reported anywhere in this study.

patient: If recovery from Lyme disease has been slow, consider raising with a clinician whether a chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or psychiatric diagnosis was considered as an alternative explanation rather than alongside a tick-borne illness evaluation - this study reported that pattern was common before a Lyme diagnosis was reached, more so among women.

Keep in mind this comes from one self-selected patient registry (recruited via blogs, social media, and clinician outreach) that the authors themselves note skews toward higher income and education, so its percentages describe that specific group, not a general prediction.

If bed days, disability, or needing mobility equipment have been part of the experience, note the study reported these as more common among women in this sample - this may be useful context to bring into a conversation about ongoing symptom management, not a diagnosis of one's own situation.
care: Consider reviewing whether intake or differential-diagnosis workflows systematically ask about tick exposure or Lyme-endemic travel before defaulting toward a chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or psychiatric diagnosis, given this study's finding of high misdiagnosis rates with those conditions before a Lyme diagnosis was reached, more so among women.

Note this study found no significant sex difference in rash recollection or positive lab test rates, while misdiagnosis rates differed significantly by sex - this gap may be worth checking against how clinical judgment versus lab results are weighted in a given workup, rather than attributing it to test-positivity differences.

package.documentation:
This simulator uses sex-disaggregated percentages reported in a peer-reviewed study analyzing the MyLymeData patient registry (dataset dated April 27, 2017), a self-selected, self-reported sample of 2,170 U.S. patients (1,839 women, 331 men) clinically diagnosed with persistent/chronic Lyme disease (illness continuing six or more months after antibiotic treatment). All inputs are percentages of patients reporting a given outcome, taken directly from Tables 3-5 (pp.5-7) and Figure 3 (p.8) of the study.

Four outputs compute percentage-point differences: a late-stage diagnosis gap, a misdiagnosis gap (prior diagnosis with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or a psychiatric condition), a functional-impairment gap (eight or more bed days in six months), and a gap between the mean share of women enrolled in acute Lyme disease study sources versus persistent-illness study sources the authors separately reviewed. The first three gaps compare women to men within the same registry sample and were reported by the study as statistically significant (p<0.05). The fourth gap compares two different groups of studies with different designs and populations, not a single underlying quantity, per the document's own framing.

This study reports no dollar-denominated medical cost, non-medical cost, or lost-income/productivity figure anywhere in its text; no cost outputs are included here for that reason.

Limitation: the study describes a research-design gap in the broader evidence base - despite a 2015 NIH mandate to include biological sex as a variable in research, the authors found that none of the NIH-funded randomized controlled trials and very few other Lyme disease clinical studies they reviewed were designed to analyze sex-based differences as part of their research design. This is a limitation of the evidence-generating system, distinct from the accuracy of this study's own reported percentages.

All findings rely on single point-in-time patient self-report with no independent clinical chart verification, and the registry sample is self-selected (recruited via blogs, social media, and clinician outreach) and skews toward higher education and income than the general population, which the authors note limits generalizability. Race/ethnicity and gender-identity-spectrum subgroup analyses could not be performed because the authors state their data did not include a sufficient sample across those groups.
